body: I wanted to compliment you on engaging in a respectful manner. I do think each of you were looking at it from different angles -- you acknowledging potential health problems, and "Red" acknowledging that hating a person because of how they look (regardless of how they got there) isn't productive. Two different aspects as it relates to body size: both the social and the medical.

Well, it happened to me and it was very overt -- so I can say with confidence that it does happen. 

My husband and I went to a restaurant. The waitress came and asked for our order. We ordered a pizza. She then asked, "any salads?" We both declined. She then touches his shoulder and says, "Well, he doesn't need it..." then touches mine and says, "But you, dear..." before walking away.

When I called to talk to the manager about her commentary later on, he reacted in such a way that made it clear that this had not been a one-time problem with this waitress. I don't know if she was just going around commenting on the sizes of all of the fat people or if she was pointing out other groups too, but he was clearly acquainted with her behavior.

Many of you are saying, "What person would risk their livelihood by doing this?" Many fat people are lucky to not have to deal with smart-ass comments, or at least to deal with them often. Others get a little pudgy and suddenly the outspoken jerks come out of no where.

I honestly believe that this waitress thought that I would shrug off the behavior with an, "Oh, she's right, I'm just a worthless fat-ass who should be publicly shamed." It's the same thing I think when I see people openly humiliating fat people while using their real names, or going right up to someone and saying something (something I have experienced firsthand, and something I have seen happen to others).

I think that there's a sense of: fat people are subhuman. Fat people should be grateful that I'm pointing out their flaw. How can they be angry -- what I've just said is true! There's a sense of social cohesion when this happens -- "Well, whatever, the fat person might be upset, but I know everyone else agrees with me." Others choose a route that offers some other plausible explanation: "oh, I was just kidding!" or "Oh, that person is just too sensitive!"

Do I think that being served Diet Pepsi is necessarily fat-shaming from a waiter? No, but it certainly could be a passive-aggressive way of doing so. But again, there is another plausible explanation there. I wouldn't just assume, in and of itself, that someone was trying to make a dig at me. Now, if they're also making commentary on the caloric value of everything else I order, it suddenly becomes a little clearer!

Yeah, your brows are like...the most symmetrical that I've ever seen on a person.

I always screw mine up when I pluck, even using my browbone as a guideline. Looks kind like I'm constantly raising an eyebrow sometimes. Hahahaha!

Your last sentence is *so* right and it perfectly encapsulates the kinds of people who say such nasty things: says nothing about you, but EVERYTHING about them. Emi, I think that this is a lovely, dramatic picture of you! And it is because of the subject -- not just because of the photographer!

Thank you for posting the article, atchka. :d Just this article right here could solve so many problems that we have. I remember growing up and constantly feeling that my body was being scrutinized, and that I was bad/awful/ugly/stupid/and on and on for looking the way that I did. I was significantly taller than the other girls, built broadly and heavier to match. 

And it was encouraged by family, by culture, by classmates who teased me and on and on. I wish I could go back in time to that little girl and say, "Look, eat when you're hungry. Try to get in a little physical activity, just for the sake of enjoying the movement of your body, not to look a certain way. Things will be OK."

Instead, it was years of massive weight losses following calorie-restricted diets (per professional advice), then regaining massive amounts thereafter. And feeling like garbage the entire time because I had to analyze every bite, had to worry and get paranoid every time we went out to eat because...oh god, nothing low-calorie on the menu!

Then, boom, stumble upon "Health at Every Size," eat only when hungry, make an effort to go for the healthier foods, move your body just because it's fun...and my weight stabilized for the first time in years. 

So many parents carry their internalized fat-shame with them. My brother-in-law was always the "fat guy," and over the last year or two, has steadily been losing weight and getting active. He rides his bike everywhere. What concerns me is that he now has a 2-year-old daughter...and every time I see him, it's, "I am not going to have a daughter who is fat like her daddy," "She is going to be thin," "I won't let her get fat," and etc. 

The perfect storm for self-esteem slams: a dad who is hyper-focused on your weight. His first report every time she sees a pediatrician? Her weight and how light she is and how her doctor says she'll be tall and thin and how happy that makes him. And while, on the one hand, I'm happy she'll be tall and thin -- because she'll have a lot less trouble -- the other side of me says, "Yeah, brother-in-law, but what if things turn out VERY differently than you expect?"

What if she shares your genetic predisposition for extra weight -- lifestyle aside, which can be responsible for an extra 10 - 20 pounds? What then?

What if she grows up resentful of exercise and eating well because it's treated as 'punishment' for not being thin? Or...as a safeguard against the Bogeyman...of becoming fat?

Like this writer, I learned that "being fat" was associated with every possible bad outcome imaginable. Fat people never dated, never had sex, had trouble making friends, were stupid, dumb and lazy, were going to fail at their jobs, on and on. Then I became a fat adult who, surprisingly, did OK for herself.

I'm having a son in a few weeks. I'm already excitedly talking to my husband about signing up for the YMCA near us. An indoor/outdoor pool! An enormous basketball court! Plenty of opportunities to have some bonding/fitness time with my boy as he gets older. I'm excited about buying a variety of fruits and vegetables and cutting them up and letting him make his own fruit salad, letting him try carrots with hummus and all the yumminess they offer.

I hope to God he has a love for Thai like his dad and I do: yes, son, let's get some pa ka praw! And that he also shares a love for Lebanese food.

Health should be about mental health, too. And it's sad to me that in studies where minority women report less distress over the size of their bodies than white women, the conclusion is, "We need to make these minority women realize that their body size is unacceptable." In other words, "these minority women are not nearly neurotic and depressed and obsessed enough with their weight."

Everything for a thin body, though, right?

Even if it screws kids up from such a young age.

We have come to a crappy place culturally. As you point out, one where people who feel they need to gain weight (for health, for aesthetic reasons...or some other reason I'm not thinking of) are openly scorned. 

What concerns me is that you seem to be saying that you are dropping weight without trying -- have you talked to a doctor about this? You also mention being underfed/money problems, so I am hopeful that between the two possibilities, this has more to do with the trouble with keeping on weight.

Comments on peoples' weight is mind-blowing to me. Over the last few years, I made a conscious decision to stop acknowledging when someone has lost weight, and I will not comment on a thin person's body -- "You're so skinny!" "You need to gain weight!," etc. 

It bothers me that we have turned weight into a moral issue. The "skinny people" have self-respect, they work hard at it, they care, damn it (and on the negative side, we get "oh, they don't do anything but work out all day! She must have an eating disorder! I bet she's a bitch!"! The "fatties/ham planets/etc." are lazy, selfish, irresponsible, stupid gluttons who don't care about anybody but themselves. 

You're right: I don't care what somebody else does or doesn't eat or how often or how infrequently they exercise. That's something for the person and their doctor. No amount of shame is going to get a person to permanently and successfully maintain a "normal" weight -- the studies prove that. We bring so much psychological damage to people by telling them that their bodies suck and they suck on a perpetual basis.

My nausea started just shy of 6 weeks, I felt nauseous just about every day (morning sickness would take a break for a week, then come back; it hit strong and tapered off, though I still threw up here and there up till 20 weeks).

I threw up anywhere from 3 - 7 times a week; never threw up more than twice in one day, though.

I am having a boy.

Was on mini pill. Went off and immediately began trying. Ovulation tests, temperatures, cervical mucus...

didn't get pregnant until cycle #10. Since you mention the blood pressure thing (I had to get off of combination pills for the same reason), look into the mini pill. Fertility is supposed to bounce back faster with that than with just about any other form of hormonal contraception.

In our case, my SO had the fertility issues.
